doc.title: Kenny Barron — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: The state of jazz, future plans and close
title: The state of the jazz business
summary: Few bookings and no recording contract, though he is writing in the gap.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Uh-oh, you done brought up the business. Let’s talk about the state of jazz today. You were so candid yesterday, off mic, to mention the fact that your schedule was open, because you didn’t have any bookings until April, and I’m thinking, damn. And then you also said, “I don’t even have a recording contract. I’m thinking, damn, this is the premier pianist alive, and it’s hard for him. The business is not there for him to support the continuation of this art form.
I don’t know the answer to that. I’m not going to starve. But yeah, I would like to be working. It’s not as grim as I painted it. I’m going to Israel this coming week, but for a day.
Wow. That’s a hell of a one-nighter.
Obviously, the whole thing will take about three or four days, but for one concert. Then in February I’m going to London, just for a three-day gig. Then I have a recording session in February.
It sounds like you still have to leave the country to get work.
Let’s make sure we get this out, so he can get some gigs.
But it’s okay, because I’m going to spend the time writing. I have some projects I would like to do. So I’m going to use the time well, I think.
